posts.title: Your IPO Is Too Important to Trust the Wrong Advisor

posts.content:

IPO advisory is one of the most consequential and specific engagements a business will ever undertake. Getting a company listed — whether on the mainboard or the SME exchange — requires someone who understands SEBI regulations in their current form, not two years ago. It requires experience with your specific sector, because a DRHP for a pharma company looks nothing like one for a logistics firm. It requires someone who has sat in those rooms before.

posts.title: Your CA Incorporated the Company. Nobody Checked the ESOP Clause.
posts.excerpt: The legal gap that kills Indian startups isn't bad advice — it's advice from someone who's never done this exact thing before.
posts.content:
Rohan Mehta had built something real. Three years, a team of eleven, a SaaS product with paying clients in four countries. His Bengaluru-based startup was finally raising its Series A — a ₹12 crore round from a Mumbai-based VC fund. The lawyers were engaged. The CA was looped in. Everyone was busy. And then, two weeks before close, the lead investor's legal team flagged something that stopped the room cold.

The ESOP pool had been structured incorrectly at incorporation. The vesting schedule was non-standard in a way that created ambiguity about whether two early employees — now critical to the business — actually held what they thought they held. The cap table had a shadow hanging over it that nobody had caught because nobody on Rohan's advisory team had ever actually structured an ESOP pool for a VC-backed startup before. His CA had incorporated hundreds of companies. His lawyer had drafted dozens of shareholder agreements. But neither of them had sat in a startup's board meeting six months before a funding round and felt what it means when the ESOP clause is wrong.

The deal did not fall through. But it was renegotiated. The valuation took a hit. Two employees had to be reissued grant letters with legal uncertainty hanging over the process. It cost Rohan four weeks, two lakhs in additional legal fees, and a piece of something harder to put a number on — the confidence of his investors going into a relationship that was supposed to start clean.

This is not a story about bad professionals. Rohan's CA is excellent. His lawyer is thorough. The gap was not competence — it was depth. Startup legal advisory in India, done right, is a specific skill set. It means knowing how the DPIIT recognition framework interacts with your cap table structure. It means knowing which shareholder agreement clauses will flag with a Sequoia term sheet versus a Chiratae one. It means having sat across from a SEBI inquiry for a founder who took convertible notes the wrong way and understanding, in your bones, what that conversation feels like. That knowledge is not in a textbook. It lives with specific people who have done this specific work.

The problem in India is not that those people don't exist. They do. The problem is that finding them is almost entirely a function of which city you're in, which college you went to, and who your investors already know. A founder in Jaipur building a fintech startup does not have the same access to a startup-specialist legal mind as a founder in Koramangala who went to IIM. Here is how it works. You go to mahayukti.com and describe your problem — specifically, in your own words. Not a form with dropdown menus. A real description of what you're dealing with. The Mahayukti team reviews it and matches you to a verified specialist whose background fits your exact need. Then you work directly with that expert — with full accountability on both sides.

Two scenarios where this matters for startup founders specifically.

First: You're a Delhi-based founder preparing for seed funding. Your existing company structure — a private limited you set up quickly in 2021 — has a clause your new investor's legal team is going to hate. You don't know that yet. Your current lawyer set it up correctly for what it was at the time, but they've never worked with a funding round. Mahayukti connects you to a startup legal specialist — someone who has worked on fifty-plus funding transactions — who reviews your structure before you get to term sheet stage and catches what needs to be fixed before it becomes a negotiation point.

Second: You're a Pune-based founder going from bootstrapped to VC-backed for the first time. You've been advised by four different people about ESOP structuring — your CA, a founder friend, a lawyer who works mostly in real estate, and a blog post from 2019. None of that advice fully agrees. You need one person who has structured ESOPs for Indian startups under the current regulatory framework, knows the tax implications for employees at exercise, and can tell you with confidence what to do. That person exists. Mahayukti finds them for you.

The reason this matters is not just that you get better advice. It's that you get advice you can act on without second-guessing. When someone has done your exact thing before — not something adjacent, not something similar — their guidance carries a different weight.
